decks.title: Equation of a Straight Line — Part 1: Slope, inclination and the forms of a line
goals: Find the inclination and slope of a line, using m = tan θ
Calculate the slope of the line through two points and test points for collinearity
Write and read the slope-intercept form y = mx + c
Find the equation of a line from a point and a slope, or from two points

slides.heading: Equation of a Straight Line, Part 1
slides.body_md: Every straight line on a graph has an **equation** in $x$ and $y$. Its **slope** tells how steep it is; its **intercepts** tell where it crosses the axes.

visual.alt: A straight line rising gently from left to right. It crosses the x-axis at A (−2, 0), the y-axis at C (0, 1), and passes through B (4, 3). Its equation is y = one half x + 1.
visual.caption: One line, one equation: $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + 1$.

slides.narration: Welcome to the equation of a straight line. Every point on this line obeys one rule linking its x and y coordinates. That rule is the equation of the line. In this part you will measure how steep a line is, and learn three ways to write its equation.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **inclination** and **slope** of a line
Calculate the slope from **two points**, and test points for **collinearity**
Write and read **$y = mx + c$**
Find the equation from a **point and a slope**, or from **two points**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we measure steepness with the inclination and the slope. Then we find the slope from two points and use it to test whether points lie on one line. Finally we write equations in three useful forms.

slides.heading: Inclination and slope
slides.body_md: The **inclination** $\theta$ of a line is the angle it makes with the **positive direction of the $x$-axis**, measured anticlockwise ($0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$). Its **slope** (gradient) is

visual.alt: Table of inclinations and slopes: 0 degrees gives slope 0, a horizontal line; 30 degrees gives 1 over root 3; 45 degrees gives 1; 60 degrees gives root 3, rising steeply; 90 degrees, a vertical line, has no slope; 135 degrees gives −1, a falling line.
visual.caption: The slope is the tangent of the inclination.

slides.narration: The inclination of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x axis, measured anticlockwise. The slope, also called the gradient, is the tangent of that angle. A horizontal line has slope zero. At forty five degrees the slope is one. A vertical line has no slope at all, because the tangent of ninety degrees is not defined.

slides.heading: Slope from two points
slides.body_md: For two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$, the slope is the **rise** divided by the **run**:

visual.alt: The line through A (−1, 1) and B (3, 4), with a right-angled step drawn under it: a horizontal run of 4 units from A, then a vertical rise of 3 units up to B. The slope is rise over run, 3 over 4.
visual.caption: Slope $=$ rise $\div$ run $= \dfrac{3}{4}$.

slides.narration: To find the slope from two points, divide the change in y, the rise, by the change in x, the run. From A to B the run is four and the rise is three, so the slope is three quarters. Take the two points in the same order on the top and the bottom.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: slope and inclination
slides.body_md: Find the slope of the line through $P(-2, 5)$ and $Q(4, -1)$, and its inclination.
bullets: **Step 2 —** $\tan \theta = -1$. A negative slope means an obtuse inclination: $\theta = 135^\circ$.
**Check —** the line falls from left to right, as a negative slope should.

visual.alt: Worked example 1: the line through P (−2, 5) and Q (4, −1) falls from left to right. Its slope is −1 and it makes an angle of 135 degrees with the positive x-axis.
visual.caption: A negative slope: the line falls from left to right.

slides.narration: Subtract in the same order: minus one minus five on top, four minus minus two below, giving minus six over six, which is minus one. A slope of minus one means the tangent of the inclination is minus one, so the angle is one hundred and thirty five degrees. The line falls from left to right.

slides.heading: What the slope tells you
bullets: $m > 0$: the line **rises** from left to right
$m < 0$: the line **falls** from left to right
$m = 0$: the line is **horizontal** ($y = k$)
a **vertical** line ($x = k$) has **no slope**: the run is $0$

visual.alt: Four lines through the point K (1, 2): y = 2x rises from left to right (slope 2); y = −x + 3 falls (slope −1); y = 2 is horizontal (slope 0); and the dashed vertical line x = 1 has no slope.
visual.caption: Rising: $m > 0$. Falling: $m < 0$. Horizontal: $m = 0$. Vertical: not defined.

slides.narration: The sign of the slope tells you the direction. A positive slope rises from left to right, and a negative slope falls. A horizontal line has slope zero. For a vertical line the run is zero, and we cannot divide by zero, so a vertical line has no slope.

slides.heading: Quick check: a missing slope
slides.body_md: Look for two points with the same $x$-coordinate.
slides.narration: Which of these lines is vertical? Look for two points with the same x coordinate.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from points to angle, and back
slides.body_md: (i) Find the inclination of the line through $A(3, 1)$ and $B(5, 3)$. (ii) Find the slope of a line inclined at $60^\circ$.
bullets: **(ii) —** $m = \tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$.
**Note —** the line in (i) meets the $x$-axis at $D(2, 0)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2: the line through A (3, 1) and B (5, 3) rises one unit for every unit across, so its slope is 1 and its inclination is 45 degrees. It crosses the x-axis at D (2, 0).
visual.caption: Slope $1$: inclination $45^\circ$.

slides.narration: For the first part, the slope is two over two, which is one. The angle whose tangent is one is forty five degrees. For the second part we go the other way: the slope of a line inclined at sixty degrees is the tangent of sixty degrees, which is root three.

slides.heading: Collinear points
slides.body_md: Three points $A$, $B$, $C$ are **collinear** (on one straight line) when the slope of $AB$ equals the slope of $BC$: the two segments have the same steepness and share the point $B$.

visual.alt: Three points U (−3, −1), V (0, 1) and W (3, 3) on one straight line. The slope from U to V and the slope from V to W are both 2 over 3.
visual.caption: Equal slopes $UV$ and $VW$, with $V$ shared: one straight line.

slides.narration: Slopes give a quick test for points on one line. If the slope from A to B equals the slope from B to C, the two segments point the same way and share B, so all three points are on one line. Here both slopes are two thirds, so U, V and W are collinear.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: an unknown coordinate
slides.body_md: The points $A(1, -1)$, $B(3, 3)$ and $C(k, 7)$ are collinear. Find $k$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** slope $BC$ must also be $2$: $\dfrac{7 - 3}{k - 3} = 2 \Rightarrow k - 3 = 2 \Rightarrow k = 5$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3: the points A (1, −1), B (3, 3) and C (5, 7) on the line y = 2x − 3. Each step of 2 units across is a rise of 4 units.
visual.caption: With $k = 5$, $C(5, 7)$ is on line $AB$.

slides.narration: First find the slope of A B: four over two, which is two. For C to be on the same line, the slope from B to C must also be two. So seven minus three, divided by k minus three, equals two. That gives k minus three equals two, and k equals five.

slides.heading: Quick check: one straight line
slides.body_md: Make the slope of $BC$ equal to the slope of $AB$.
slides.narration: Find the slope of A B first. Then make the slope of B C equal to it.

slides.heading: Slope-intercept form
slides.body_md: A line with slope $m$ that cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, c)$ has the equation
bullets: $c$ is the **$y$-intercept**
a line through the origin has $c = 0$: $y = mx$
to **read** $m$ and $c$ from $ax + by + c = 0$, make $y$ the subject

visual.alt: The line y = two thirds x − 2. It crosses the y-axis at C (0, −2), so its y-intercept is −2; it crosses the x-axis at D (3, 0) and passes through E (6, 2). Every 3 units across it rises 2 units.
visual.caption: In $y = mx + c$: slope $m = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $y$-intercept $c = -2$.

slides.narration: If you know the slope and where the line cuts the y axis, the equation is y equals m x plus c. Here m is the slope and c is the y intercept. This line has slope two thirds and cuts the y axis at minus two. A line through the origin has c equal to zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: writing and reading y = mx + c
slides.body_md: (i) Find the equation of the line with slope $-\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $y$-intercept $4$. (ii) Find the slope and $y$-intercept of $3x - 4y + 8 = 0$.
bullets: **(i) —** $y = -\dfrac{2}{3}x + 4 \Rightarrow 3y = -2x + 12 \Rightarrow 2x + 3y - 12 = 0$.
**(ii) —** make $y$ the subject: $4y = 3x + 8 \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{3}{4}x + 2$.
**Answer —** (ii) has slope $\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $y$-intercept $2$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4: the falling line 2x + 3y − 12 = 0, which meets the y-axis at P (0, 4), and the rising line 3x − 4y + 8 = 0, which meets the y-axis at Q (0, 2).
visual.caption: The constant in $y = mx + c$ is where the line meets the $y$-axis.

slides.narration: For the first part, put m and c straight into y equals m x plus c, then multiply by three to clear the fraction: two x plus three y minus twelve equals zero. For the second part, move the y term across and divide by four. The slope is three quarters and the y intercept is two.

slides.heading: Point-slope form
slides.body_md: If a line has slope $m$ and passes through $(x_1, y_1)$, then every other point $(x, y)$ on it gives $\dfrac{y - y_1}{x - x_1} = m$, so
bullets: For $A(2, 1)$ and $m = 3$: $y - 1 = 3(x - 2)$, that is $y = 3x - 5$; the point $B(3, 4)$ checks: $\dfrac{4 - 1}{3 - 2} = 3$.

visual.alt: The line of slope 3 through A (2, 1). Any other point on it, such as B (3, 4), gives the same slope with A: a rise of 3 for a run of 1.
visual.caption: Every point $(x, y)$ of the line gives slope $3$ with $A$.

slides.narration: Suppose you know one point on a line and its slope. Any other point on the line makes the same slope with the known point. Writing that down gives y minus y one equals m times x minus x one. This is the point slope form, the most useful form of all.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a point and a slope
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through $(2, -3)$ with slope $\dfrac{3}{2}$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $y + 3 = \dfrac{3}{2}(x - 2) \Rightarrow 2y + 6 = 3x - 6 \Rightarrow 3x - 2y - 12 = 0$.
**Check —** substitute $(2, -3)$: $3 \times 2 - 2 \times (-3) - 12 = 0$.
**Note —** it meets the axes at $(4, 0)$ and $(0, -6)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 5: the line 3x − 2y − 12 = 0 of slope 3 over 2 through A (2, −3). It crosses the x-axis at D (4, 0) and the y-axis at E (0, −6).
visual.caption: Point-slope form, then clear the fraction.

slides.narration: Put the point and the slope into the point slope form: y plus three equals three halves of x minus two. Multiply both sides by two to clear the fraction, then collect everything on one side: three x minus two y minus twelve equals zero. Always check by substituting the given point.

slides.heading: Two-point form
slides.body_md: Two points fix a line. Find the slope from the points, then use the point-slope form with either point:

visual.alt: Flow chart for the line through two points: find the slope from the two points, write the point-slope form with either point, clear the fractions to get the form a x + b y + c = 0, then check by substituting the other point.
visual.caption: Two points fix the slope; either point then fixes the line.

slides.narration: When you are given two points, first work out the slope from them. Then use the point slope form with either point. Clear the fractions and write the equation neatly. Finally check it with the other point: if both points satisfy the equation, it is correct.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: two points
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through $A(-1, 4)$ and $B(3, -2)$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** with $A$: $y - 4 = -\dfrac{3}{2}(x + 1) \Rightarrow 2y - 8 = -3x - 3 \Rightarrow 3x + 2y - 5 = 0$.
**Check —** with $B$: $3 \times 3 + 2 \times (-2) - 5 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6: the falling line 3x + 2y − 5 = 0 through A (−1, 4) and B (3, −2).
visual.caption: Both given points satisfy $3x + 2y - 5 = 0$.

slides.narration: The slope is minus two minus four over three minus minus one, which is minus six over four, or minus three halves. Using A, y minus four equals minus three halves of x plus one. Multiply by two and tidy up: three x plus two y minus five equals zero. B checks: nine minus four minus five is zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: through two points
slides.body_md: Find the slope, then the $y$-intercept.
slides.narration: Find the slope first. One of the points lies on the y axis, which gives you c at once.

slides.heading: Intercepts, and points on a line
slides.body_md: A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates **satisfy** the equation.
bullets: **$x$-intercept:** put $y = 0$
**$y$-intercept:** put $x = 0$
For $4x + 3y = 12$: $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$; the triangle with the axes has area $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6$; and $T(6, -4)$ is on the line, since $4 \times 6 + 3 \times (-4) = 12$.

visual.alt: The line 4x + 3y = 12 crossing the x-axis at A (3, 0) and the y-axis at B (0, 4). The point T (6, −4) also satisfies the equation, so it lies on the line.
visual.caption: Put $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept and $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept.

slides.narration: To find where a line crosses the x axis, put y equal to zero. To find where it crosses the y axis, put x equal to zero. And to test whether a point lies on a line, substitute its coordinates. If the equation is satisfied, the point is on the line.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Put $x = 0$ and solve for $y$.
slides.narration: Where does this line cross the y axis? Put x equal to zero and solve.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Slope $m = \tan \theta$; $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$
Collinear points: equal slopes
Slope-intercept form $y = mx + c$
Point-slope form $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$; two points: find $m$ first
Intercepts: put $y = 0$ or $x = 0$

visual.alt: Summary table of the forms: slope from two points, slope as tan theta, slope-intercept form y = m x + c, point-slope form, two-point form, and the general form a x + b y + c = 0 with slope minus a over b and y-intercept minus c over b.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. The slope is the tangent of the inclination, or rise over run between two points. Equal slopes show that points are collinear. A line can be written as y equals m x plus c, or with the point slope form. To find intercepts, put y or x equal to zero.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Slope (1 mark):** formula with the coordinates substituted in the same order
**Equation (2–3 marks):** slope 1, point-slope form 1, simplified form 1
**Inclination:** use $\tan \theta = m$; a negative slope gives an obtuse angle
**Mistake:** $\dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_1 - x_2}$ (mixed order) changes the sign
**Mistake:** reading the slope of $ax + by + c = 0$ as $a$; it is $-\dfrac{a}{b}$
**Habit:** check your equation with the given points
slides.narration: In the exam, write the slope formula with the numbers substituted, keeping the same order on top and bottom. For an equation, show the slope, the point slope form, and then the simplified answer. A common slip is reading the slope of a x plus b y plus c equals zero as a. Make y the subject first. And always check with the given points.

decks.title: Equation of a Straight Line — Part 2: Parallel and perpendicular lines, and applications
goals: Test whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular using their slopes
Find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line
Find unknown coefficients and the meeting point of two lines
Find the perpendicular bisector, median and altitude using the mid-point and section formulae

slides.heading: Equation of a Straight Line, Part 2
slides.body_md: Slopes tell us when two lines are **parallel** and when they meet at **right angles**. With the mid-point and section formulae, they find the special lines of a triangle.

visual.alt: Two parallel rising lines, y = 2x − 1 and y = 2x + 4, cut at right angles by the falling line y = −one half x + 4, which meets them at P (2, 3) and Q (0, 4).
visual.caption: Equal slopes: parallel. Slopes multiplying to $-1$: perpendicular.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here two rising lines with the same slope run side by side, and a third line cuts both at right angles. In this part we use slopes to spot parallel and perpendicular lines, and then combine them with the mid-point and section formulae.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Test lines for being **parallel** or **perpendicular**
Find a line **parallel** or **perpendicular** to a given line through a point
Find **unknown coefficients** and the **meeting point** of two lines
Find **perpendicular bisectors**, **medians** and **altitudes**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We test pairs of lines, write lines parallel or perpendicular to a given one, find unknown coefficients and meeting points, and finish with the special lines of a triangle.

slides.heading: Parallel lines
slides.body_md: Two non-vertical lines are **parallel** exactly when they have **equal slopes**:
bullets: equal slopes mean equal inclinations
parallel lines have **different** intercepts (equal intercepts would make them the same line)
any two vertical lines are parallel

visual.alt: Two parallel lines with the same slope one third: y = one third x + 2 through A (0, 2) and y = one third x − 1 through B (0, −1). They never meet.
visual.caption: Same slope, different intercepts: parallel lines.

slides.narration: Parallel lines have the same steepness, so they have the same slope. These two lines both have slope one third, but they cut the y axis at different points, so they never meet. If the intercepts were also equal, they would be the same line. Any two vertical lines are parallel too.

slides.heading: Perpendicular lines
slides.body_md: Two lines, neither vertical, are **perpendicular** exactly when the **product of their slopes is $-1$**:
bullets: so a perpendicular slope is the **negative reciprocal**: $-\dfrac{1}{m}$
here $\dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -1$
a horizontal line and a vertical line are also perpendicular

visual.alt: The line 3x − 2y + 2 = 0 through A (0, 1), of slope 3 over 2, and the line 2x + 3y − 16 = 0 through B (5, 2), of slope −2 over 3. They cross at right angles at M (2, 4).
visual.caption: $\dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -1$: the lines are perpendicular.

slides.narration: Lines that meet at right angles have slopes whose product is minus one. So to get a perpendicular slope, turn the slope upside down and change its sign. Three halves becomes minus two thirds. The only exception is a horizontal line with a vertical line, which are perpendicular although the vertical one has no slope.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: parallel, perpendicular or neither?
bullets: **Step 1 —** the slope of $ax + by + c = 0$ is $-\dfrac{a}{b}$.
**Step 2 —** compare: equal slopes, or a product of $-1$.
**Answers —** (i) parallel; (ii) perpendicular; (iii) neither.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1 of part 2: 3x − 2y + 5 = 0 and 6x − 4y − 7 = 0 both have slope 3 over 2, so they are parallel; 2x + 5y − 7 = 0 and 5x − 2y + 3 = 0 have slopes −2 over 5 and 5 over 2, product −1, so they are perpendicular; x + 2y − 4 = 0 and 2x + y + 1 = 0 have slopes −1 over 2 and −2, product 1, so they are neither.
visual.caption: Compare slopes: equal, product $-1$, or neither.

slides.narration: Find each slope as minus a over b. In the first pair both slopes are three halves, so the lines are parallel. In the second pair the slopes are minus two fifths and five halves, whose product is minus one, so they are perpendicular. In the third pair the product is plus one, so they are neither.

slides.heading: Quick check: a parallel line
slides.body_md: Which line has the same slope?
slides.narration: Find the slope of the given line, then look for the option with the same slope.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a parallel line through a point
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through $(3, -2)$ parallel to $4x - y + 7 = 0$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the given line is $y = 4x + 7$, so its slope is $4$; the parallel line has slope $4$ too.
**Step 2 —** $y + 2 = 4(x - 3) \Rightarrow y + 2 = 4x - 12 \Rightarrow 4x - y - 14 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 2 of part 2: the given line 4x − y + 7 = 0 through G (0, 7) and the parallel line 4x − y − 14 = 0 through A (3, −2). Both have slope 4.
visual.caption: Parallel: copy the slope, change the point.

slides.narration: First find the slope of the given line by making y the subject: y equals four x plus seven, so the slope is four. The parallel line has the same slope. Put slope four and the point three, minus two into the point slope form, and tidy up: four x minus y minus fourteen equals zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a perpendicular line through a point
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through $A(-2, 1)$ perpendicular to $x + 3y - 6 = 0$, and the foot of the perpendicular.
bullets: **Step 1 —** the given slope is $-\dfrac{1}{3}$, so the perpendicular slope is $3$.
**Step 2 —** $y - 1 = 3(x + 2) \Rightarrow 3x - y + 7 = 0$.

**Step 3 —** foot: put $y = 3x + 7$ into $x + 3y - 6 = 0$: $x + 3(3x + 7) - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow 10x = -15 \Rightarrow x = -\dfrac{3}{2}$; then $y = 3 \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + 7 = \dfrac{5}{2}$, giving $F\left(-\dfrac{3}{2}, \dfrac{5}{2}\right)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 3 of part 2: the falling line x + 3y − 6 = 0 and the steep line 3x − y + 7 = 0 through A (−2, 1), perpendicular to it. They meet at F (−3/2, 5/2), the foot of the perpendicular from A.
visual.caption: Slopes $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $3$ multiply to $-1$.

slides.narration: The given line has slope minus one third. Turn it upside down and change the sign: the perpendicular slope is three. Through A, that gives three x minus y plus seven equals zero. The foot of the perpendicular is where the two lines meet, so solve them together. It is minus three halves, five halves.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an unknown coefficient
slides.body_md: For what values of $k$ is the line $kx + 2y - 5 = 0$ (i) parallel, (ii) perpendicular to $3x - y + 1 = 0$?
bullets: **Step 1 —** slopes: $-\dfrac{k}{2}$ and $3$.
**(i) —** equal slopes: $-\dfrac{k}{2} = 3 \Rightarrow k = -6$.
**(ii) —** product $-1$: $-\dfrac{k}{2} \times 3 = -1 \Rightarrow k = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

visual.alt: Worked example 4 of part 2: the fixed line 3x − y + 1 = 0 through A (0, 1); the line for k = −6, parallel to it; and the line for k = two thirds, perpendicular to it. Both lines with k pass through B (0, 5/2).
visual.caption: Parallel when $k = -6$; perpendicular when $k = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

slides.narration: Write both slopes. The first line has slope minus k over two, and the second has slope three. For parallel lines set them equal: minus k over two equals three, so k is minus six. For perpendicular lines set their product equal to minus one: that gives k equals two thirds.

slides.heading: Quick check: at right angles
slides.body_md: Set the product of the slopes equal to $-1$.
slides.narration: Write the two slopes, then set their product equal to minus one.

slides.heading: Where two lines meet
slides.body_md: The meeting point of two lines satisfies **both** equations, so solve them **simultaneously** (substitution or elimination).
bullets: $x + y = 5$ and $x - 2y = -1$: substitute $x = 5 - y$: $(5 - y) - 2y = -1 \Rightarrow 3y = 6 \Rightarrow y = 2$, then $x = 3$.
parallel lines have no meeting point

visual.alt: The lines x + y = 5 and x − 2y = −1 drawn on one graph. They cross at P (3, 2), the only point whose coordinates satisfy both equations.
visual.caption: The meeting point satisfies both equations.

slides.narration: The point where two lines cross lies on both of them, so its coordinates satisfy both equations. Solve the two equations together, by substitution or by elimination. Here we replace x by five minus y in the second equation and find y equals two, then x equals three.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a line through a meeting point
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the line through the meeting point of $2x + y - 7 = 0$ and $x - y + 1 = 0$, perpendicular to $3x - 4y + 2 = 0$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** add the equations: $3x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2$; then $y = 2 + 1 = 3$, so $P(2, 3)$.
**Step 2 —** the given line has slope $\dfrac{3}{4}$, so the required slope is $-\dfrac{4}{3}$.
**Step 3 —** $y - 3 = -\dfrac{4}{3}(x - 2) \Rightarrow 3y - 9 = -4x + 8 \Rightarrow 4x + 3y - 17 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 5 of part 2: the lines 2x + y − 7 = 0 and x − y + 1 = 0 meet at P (2, 3). The answer line 4x + 3y − 17 = 0 also passes through P.
visual.caption: First the meeting point, then the slope.

slides.narration: Adding the two equations removes y and gives three x minus six equals zero, so x is two and y is three. The line three x minus four y plus two equals zero has slope three quarters, so the perpendicular slope is minus four thirds. Through two, three, the answer is four x plus three y minus seventeen equals zero.

slides.heading: Tools from the section and mid-point formulae
slides.body_md: Many problems need a **point** first (a mid-point, a section point or the centroid) and a **slope** second. Then the point-slope form finishes the job.

visual.alt: Table of tools: the mid-point formula, the section formula for a point dividing A B in the ratio m to n, the centroid formula, and three special lines of a triangle: the perpendicular bisector through the mid-point at right angles, the median from a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side, and the altitude from a vertex at right angles to the opposite side.
visual.caption: Find the point, find the slope, then use the point-slope form.

slides.narration: Here are the tools we combine. The mid-point formula, the section formula and the centroid give us points. The three special lines of a triangle are the perpendicular bisector, the median and the altitude. Each needs a point and a slope, and then the point slope form gives the equation.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a perpendicular bisector
slides.body_md: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $A(-1, 3)$ and $B(5, -1)$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** slope $AB = \dfrac{-1 - 3}{5 - (-1)} = \dfrac{-4}{6} = -\dfrac{2}{3}$, so the bisector has slope $\dfrac{3}{2}$.
**Step 3 —** $y - 1 = \dfrac{3}{2}(x - 2) \Rightarrow 2y - 2 = 3x - 6 \Rightarrow 3x - 2y - 4 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 6 of part 2: the segment from A (−1, 3) to B (5, −1), and its perpendicular bisector 3x − 2y − 4 = 0 crossing it at right angles at the mid-point M (2, 1).
visual.caption: Every point of the bisector is equally far from $A$ and $B$.

slides.narration: The perpendicular bisector passes through the mid-point of A B and is at right angles to it. The mid-point is two, one. The slope of A B is minus two thirds, so the bisector has slope three halves. Through two, one, the bisector is three x minus two y minus four equals zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a median and an altitude
slides.body_md: Triangle $PQR$ has $P(-2, -1)$, $Q(4, 1)$, $R(2, 5)$. Find (i) the median from $R$, (ii) the altitude from $P$.
bullets: **(i) —** mid-point of $PQ$: $\dfrac{-2 + 4}{2} = 1$ and $\dfrac{-1 + 1}{2} = 0$, so $M(1, 0)$; slope $RM = \dfrac{5 - 0}{2 - 1} = 5$; median $y - 0 = 5(x - 1) \Rightarrow 5x - y - 5 = 0$.
**(ii) —** slope $QR = \dfrac{5 - 1}{2 - 4} = -2$, so the altitude has slope $\dfrac{1}{2}$: $y + 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x + 2) \Rightarrow 2y + 2 = x + 2 \Rightarrow x - 2y = 0$.
**Note —** the altitude meets $QR$ at $F\left(\dfrac{18}{5}, \dfrac{9}{5}\right)$.

visual.alt: Worked example 7 of part 2: triangle P (−2, −1), Q (4, 1), R (2, 5). The median from R runs to M (1, 0), the mid-point of PQ. The altitude from P meets QR at right angles at F (18/5, 9/5).
visual.caption: Median: to the mid-point. Altitude: at right angles.

slides.narration: The median from R goes to the mid-point of the opposite side P Q, which is one, zero. Its slope is five, giving five x minus y minus five equals zero. The altitude from P is perpendicular to Q R. Q R has slope minus two, so the altitude has slope one half, giving x minus two y equals zero.

slides.heading: Quick check: a median
slides.body_md: First find the mid-point of the opposite side.
slides.narration: A median joins a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side. Find that mid-point first.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: the section formula and a perpendicular
slides.body_md: The line $x + 2y = 6$ meets the axes at $A$ and $B$. $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $2 : 1$. Find the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $A(6, 0)$ and $B(0, 3)$. Section formula: $x = \dfrac{2 \times 0 + 1 \times 6}{2 + 1} = 2$, $y = \dfrac{2 \times 3 + 1 \times 0}{2 + 1} = 2$, so $P(2, 2)$.
**Step 2 —** $AB$ has slope $-\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the perpendicular has slope $2$.
**Step 3 —** $y - 2 = 2(x - 2) \Rightarrow 2x - y - 2 = 0$.

visual.alt: Worked example 8 of part 2: the line x + 2y = 6 meets the x-axis at A (6, 0) and the y-axis at B (0, 3). P (2, 2) divides AB in the ratio 2 to 1, and the line 2x − y − 2 = 0 passes through P at right angles to AB.
visual.caption: Section formula for the point, negative reciprocal for the slope.

slides.narration: Putting y and then x equal to zero gives A at six, zero and B at zero, three. The section formula with ratio two to one gives P at two, two. The line A B has slope minus one half, so the perpendicular slope is two. Through P, the answer is two x minus y minus two equals zero.

bullets: Parallel: $m_1 = m_2$
Perpendicular: $m_1 m_2 = -1$, slope $-\dfrac{1}{m}$
Unknown coefficient: use one of these conditions
Meeting point: solve the equations together
Perpendicular bisector, median, altitude: a point, a slope, then point-slope form

rows: set the slopes equal, or their product to $-1$
mid-point of the opposite side; perpendicular to it

visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

notes.title: Equation of a Straight Line — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Inclination and slope
sections.body_md:
- The **inclination** $\theta$ of a line is the angle from the positive $x$-axis to the line, measured anticlockwise, with $0^\circ \le \theta < 180^\circ$.
- The **slope** (gradient) is $m = \tan \theta$.
- $m > 0$: the line rises from left to right; $m < 0$: it falls (obtuse $\theta$); $m = 0$: horizontal; a vertical line ($\theta = 90^\circ$) has no slope.

*Example:* a line inclined at $60^\circ$ has slope $\sqrt{3}$; a line of slope $-1$ has inclination $135^\circ$.

key_terms.definition_md: The angle $\theta$ a line makes with the positive direction of the $x$-axis, measured anticlockwise.
The tangent of the inclination, $m = \tan \theta$; it measures steepness.

visual.alt: Table of inclinations and slopes: 0 degrees gives slope 0, a horizontal line; 30 degrees gives 1 over root 3; 45 degrees gives 1; 60 degrees gives root 3, rising steeply; 90 degrees, a vertical line, has no slope; 135 degrees gives −1, a falling line.
visual.caption: The slope is the tangent of the inclination.

visuals.alt: Four lines through the point K (1, 2): y = 2x rises from left to right (slope 2); y = −x + 3 falls (slope −1); y = 2 is horizontal (slope 0); and the dashed vertical line x = 1 has no slope.
visuals.caption: Rising: $m > 0$. Falling: $m < 0$. Horizontal: $m = 0$. Vertical: not defined.

sections.heading: 2. Slope from two points; collinear points
sections.body_md:
- For $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ with $x_1 \ne x_2$: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, the rise divided by the run. Keep the same order on top and bottom.
- If $x_1 = x_2$ the line is vertical and has no slope.
- $A$, $B$, $C$ are **collinear** when slope $AB$ = slope $BC$.

*Example:* $P(-2, 5)$ and $Q(4, -1)$: $m = \dfrac{-1 - 5}{4 - (-2)} = -1$. For $A(1, -1)$, $B(3, 3)$, $C(k, 7)$ to be collinear, $\dfrac{7 - 3}{k - 3} = 2$, so $k = 5$.

key_terms.definition_md: The change in $y$ and the change in $x$ between two points of a line.

visual.alt: The line through A (−1, 1) and B (3, 4), with a right-angled step drawn under it: a horizontal run of 4 units from A, then a vertical rise of 3 units up to B. The slope is rise over run, 3 over 4.
visual.caption: Slope $=$ rise $\div$ run $= \dfrac{3}{4}$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 1: the line through P (−2, 5) and Q (4, −1) falls from left to right. Its slope is −1 and it makes an angle of 135 degrees with the positive x-axis.
visuals.caption: A negative slope: the line falls from left to right.

visuals.alt: Three points U (−3, −1), V (0, 1) and W (3, 3) on one straight line. The slope from U to V and the slope from V to W are both 2 over 3.
visuals.caption: Equal slopes $UV$ and $VW$, with $V$ shared: one straight line.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3: the points A (1, −1), B (3, 3) and C (5, 7) on the line y = 2x − 3. Each step of 2 units across is a rise of 4 units.
visuals.caption: With $k = 5$, $C(5, 7)$ is on line $AB$.

sections.heading: 3. Slope-intercept form and intercepts
sections.body_md:
- **$y = mx + c$**: slope $m$, $y$-intercept $c$ (the line meets the $y$-axis at $(0, c)$). A line through the origin is $y = mx$.
- From $ax + by + c = 0$ ($b \ne 0$): $y = -\dfrac{a}{b}x - \dfrac{c}{b}$, so the slope is $-\dfrac{a}{b}$ and the $y$-intercept is $-\dfrac{c}{b}$.
- **Intercepts:** put $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept and $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept.
- A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.

*Example:* $3x - 4y + 8 = 0$ gives $y = \dfrac{3}{4}x + 2$: slope $\dfrac{3}{4}$, $y$-intercept $2$. The line $4x + 3y = 12$ meets the axes at $(3, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$.

key_terms.definition_md: The $y$-coordinate $c$ of the point where a line meets the $y$-axis.
The $x$-coordinate of the point where a line meets the $x$-axis.

visual.alt: The line y = two thirds x − 2. It crosses the y-axis at C (0, −2), so its y-intercept is −2; it crosses the x-axis at D (3, 0) and passes through E (6, 2). Every 3 units across it rises 2 units.
visual.caption: In $y = mx + c$: slope $m = \dfrac{2}{3}$, $y$-intercept $c = -2$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4: the falling line 2x + 3y − 12 = 0, which meets the y-axis at P (0, 4), and the rising line 3x − 4y + 8 = 0, which meets the y-axis at Q (0, 2).
visuals.caption: The constant in $y = mx + c$ is where the line meets the $y$-axis.

visuals.alt: The line 4x + 3y = 12 crossing the x-axis at A (3, 0) and the y-axis at B (0, 4). The point T (6, −4) also satisfies the equation, so it lies on the line.
visuals.caption: Put $y = 0$ for the $x$-intercept and $x = 0$ for the $y$-intercept.

sections.heading: 4. Point-slope and two-point forms
sections.body_md:
- **Point-slope form:** the line through $(x_1, y_1)$ with slope $m$ is $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.
- **Two-point form:** find $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$, then use the point-slope form with either point.
- Clear fractions and write the answer as $ax + by + c = 0$ (or $y = mx + c$); check it with the given points.
- Special cases: a line through $(x_1, y_1)$ parallel to the $x$-axis is $y = y_1$; parallel to the $y$-axis, $x = x_1$.

*Example:* through $(2, -3)$ with slope $\dfrac{3}{2}$: $2y + 6 = 3x - 6$, so $3x - 2y - 12 = 0$. Through $(-1, 4)$ and $(3, -2)$: $m = -\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $3x + 2y - 5 = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, the line through $(x_1, y_1)$ with slope $m$.

visual.alt: The line of slope 3 through A (2, 1). Any other point on it, such as B (3, 4), gives the same slope with A: a rise of 3 for a run of 1.
visual.caption: Every point $(x, y)$ of the line gives slope $3$ with $A$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 5: the line 3x − 2y − 12 = 0 of slope 3 over 2 through A (2, −3). It crosses the x-axis at D (4, 0) and the y-axis at E (0, −6).
visuals.caption: Point-slope form, then clear the fraction.

visuals.alt: Flow chart for the line through two points: find the slope from the two points, write the point-slope form with either point, clear the fractions to get the form a x + b y + c = 0, then check by substituting the other point.
visuals.caption: Two points fix the slope; either point then fixes the line.

visuals.alt: Worked example 6: the falling line 3x + 2y − 5 = 0 through A (−1, 4) and B (3, −2).
visuals.caption: Both given points satisfy $3x + 2y - 5 = 0$.

sections.heading: 5. Parallel and perpendicular lines
sections.body_md:
- **Parallel:** $m_1 = m_2$ (and different intercepts). Two vertical lines are parallel.
- **Perpendicular:** $m_1 m_2 = -1$, so the perpendicular slope is $-\dfrac{1}{m}$. A horizontal and a vertical line are perpendicular.
- A line parallel to $ax + by + c = 0$ can be written $ax + by + k = 0$; find $k$ from the point it passes through.
- **Unknown coefficients:** set the slopes equal (parallel) or their product equal to $-1$ (perpendicular).

*Example:* through $(3, -2)$ parallel to $4x - y + 7 = 0$: $4x - y - 14 = 0$. Through $(-2, 1)$ perpendicular to $x + 3y - 6 = 0$: slope $3$, so $3x - y + 7 = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: Lines with equal slopes (or both vertical); they never meet.
For slope $m \ne 0$, the slope $-\dfrac{1}{m}$ of a perpendicular line.

visual.alt: The line 3x − 2y + 2 = 0 through A (0, 1), of slope 3 over 2, and the line 2x + 3y − 16 = 0 through B (5, 2), of slope −2 over 3. They cross at right angles at M (2, 4).
visual.caption: $\dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -1$: the lines are perpendicular.

visuals.alt: Two parallel lines with the same slope one third: y = one third x + 2 through A (0, 2) and y = one third x − 1 through B (0, −1). They never meet.
visuals.caption: Same slope, different intercepts: parallel lines.

visuals.alt: Table for worked example 1 of part 2: 3x − 2y + 5 = 0 and 6x − 4y − 7 = 0 both have slope 3 over 2, so they are parallel; 2x + 5y − 7 = 0 and 5x − 2y + 3 = 0 have slopes −2 over 5 and 5 over 2, product −1, so they are perpendicular; x + 2y − 4 = 0 and 2x + y + 1 = 0 have slopes −1 over 2 and −2, product 1, so they are neither.
visuals.caption: Compare slopes: equal, product $-1$, or neither.

visuals.alt: Worked example 2 of part 2: the given line 4x − y + 7 = 0 through G (0, 7) and the parallel line 4x − y − 14 = 0 through A (3, −2). Both have slope 4.
visuals.caption: Parallel: copy the slope, change the point.

visuals.alt: Worked example 3 of part 2: the falling line x + 3y − 6 = 0 and the steep line 3x − y + 7 = 0 through A (−2, 1), perpendicular to it. They meet at F (−3/2, 5/2), the foot of the perpendicular from A.
visuals.caption: Slopes $-\dfrac{1}{3}$ and $3$ multiply to $-1$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 4 of part 2: the fixed line 3x − y + 1 = 0 through A (0, 1); the line for k = −6, parallel to it; and the line for k = two thirds, perpendicular to it. Both lines with k pass through B (0, 5/2).
visuals.caption: Parallel when $k = -6$; perpendicular when $k = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

sections.heading: 6. The meeting point of two lines
sections.body_md:
- The point where two lines meet satisfies both equations: solve them simultaneously by substitution or elimination.
- To find a line through the meeting point with a given condition, find the point first, then the slope, then use the point-slope form.
- The **foot of the perpendicular** from a point to a line is where the perpendicular through the point meets the line.

*Example:* $2x + y - 7 = 0$ and $x - y + 1 = 0$ meet at $(2, 3)$; the line through $(2, 3)$ perpendicular to $3x - 4y + 2 = 0$ is $4x + 3y - 17 = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: The pair $(x, y)$ satisfying both equations: the meeting point of the two lines.
The point where a perpendicular from a point meets the given line.

visual.alt: The lines x + y = 5 and x − 2y = −1 drawn on one graph. They cross at P (3, 2), the only point whose coordinates satisfy both equations.
visual.caption: The meeting point satisfies both equations.

visuals.alt: Worked example 5 of part 2: the lines 2x + y − 7 = 0 and x − y + 1 = 0 meet at P (2, 3). The answer line 4x + 3y − 17 = 0 also passes through P.
visuals.caption: First the meeting point, then the slope.

sections.heading: 7. Applications: perpendicular bisector, median and altitude
sections.body_md:
- **Perpendicular bisector of $AB$:** through the mid-point of $AB$, slope $-\dfrac{1}{m_{AB}}$. Every point on it is equidistant from $A$ and $B$.
- **Median from $A$:** the line through $A$ and the mid-point of $BC$. The three medians meet at the centroid.
- **Altitude from $A$:** through $A$, perpendicular to $BC$ (slope $-\dfrac{1}{m_{BC}}$).
- With the **section formula**, a point dividing $AB$ in $m : n$ is $\left(\dfrac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n}, \dfrac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n}\right)$.

*Example:* for $A(-1, 3)$ and $B(5, -1)$ the perpendicular bisector is $3x - 2y - 4 = 0$; for $P(-2, -1)$, $Q(4, 1)$, $R(2, 5)$ the median from $R$ is $5x - y - 5 = 0$ and the altitude from $P$ is $x - 2y = 0$.

key_terms.definition_md: The line through the mid-point of a segment, at right angles to it.
The line from a vertex of a triangle to the mid-point of the opposite side.
The line from a vertex of a triangle perpendicular to the opposite side.

visual.alt: Table of tools: the mid-point formula, the section formula for a point dividing A B in the ratio m to n, the centroid formula, and three special lines of a triangle: the perpendicular bisector through the mid-point at right angles, the median from a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side, and the altitude from a vertex at right angles to the opposite side.
visual.caption: Find the point, find the slope, then use the point-slope form.

visuals.alt: Worked example 6 of part 2: the segment from A (−1, 3) to B (5, −1), and its perpendicular bisector 3x − 2y − 4 = 0 crossing it at right angles at the mid-point M (2, 1).
visuals.caption: Every point of the bisector is equally far from $A$ and $B$.

visuals.alt: Worked example 7 of part 2: triangle P (−2, −1), Q (4, 1), R (2, 5). The median from R runs to M (1, 0), the mid-point of PQ. The altitude from P meets QR at right angles at F (18/5, 9/5).
visuals.caption: Median: to the mid-point. Altitude: at right angles.

visuals.alt: Worked example 8 of part 2: the line x + 2y = 6 meets the x-axis at A (6, 0) and the y-axis at B (0, 3). P (2, 2) divides AB in the ratio 2 to 1, and the line 2x − y − 2 = 0 passes through P at right angles to AB.
visuals.caption: Section formula for the point, negative reciprocal for the slope.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Slope or inclination (1–2 marks):* formula with the values substituted 1; value (and angle) 1.
- *Equation of a line (2–3 marks):* slope 1; point-slope form 1; simplified equation 1.
- *Parallel or perpendicular line (3 marks):* given slope, new slope, equation.
- *Median, altitude or perpendicular bisector (3–4 marks):* the point (mid-point, section point) 1–2; the slope 1; the equation 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually 3 + 3 + 4; show every slope, point and substitution.

**Common mistakes**
1. Mixing the order in the slope formula: $\dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_1 - x_2}$ has the wrong sign.
2. Reading the slope of $ax + by + c = 0$ as $a$ or $\dfrac{a}{b}$; it is $-\dfrac{a}{b}$.
3. Using $-m$ or $\dfrac{1}{m}$ for a perpendicular slope instead of $-\dfrac{1}{m}$.
4. Confusing a median (to the mid-point) with an altitude (at right angles).
5. Writing a vertical line as $y = k$ or giving it a slope.
6. Not checking the final equation with the given points.

questions.stem_md: A straight line makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with the positive direction of the $x$-axis. What is its slope?
questions.solution_md: The slope is the tangent of the inclination: $m = \tan 45^\circ = 1$. Option (b) is $\tan 60^\circ$, (c) is $\tan 30^\circ$ and (d) is the slope of a horizontal line.

questions.stem_md: What is the gradient of the segment that runs from $(2, -3)$ to $(6, 5)$?
questions.solution_md: Rise over run: $m = \dfrac{5 - (-3)}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$. Option (c) divides the run by the rise, (d) subtracts the $y$-values and the $x$-values in opposite orders, and (a) adds the $x$-coordinates instead of subtracting them.

questions.stem_md: For which of these lines is the slope not defined?
questions.solution_md: When two points share their $x$-coordinate, $x_2 - x_1 = 0$ and the slope formula would divide by zero: the line $x = 3$ is vertical and has no slope. Option (d) is horizontal, with slope $0$; (a) and (b) have slopes $1$ and $3$.

questions.stem_md: Compare $y = -4x + 7$ with $y = mx + c$. Which pair gives its slope and its $y$-intercept?
questions.solution_md: In $y = mx + c$ the coefficient of $x$ is the slope and the constant term is the $y$-intercept, signs included: $m = -4$ and $c = 7$. Option (a) swaps them; (b) and (c) each drop a sign.

questions.stem_md: The gradient of the line $5x - 2y + 6 = 0$ equals
questions.solution_md: Make $y$ the subject: $2y = 5x + 6 \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{5}{2}x + 3$, so $m = \dfrac{5}{2}$. Option (b) drops the minus sign of the $y$-term, (c) turns the fraction upside down and (d) is only the coefficient of $x$.

questions.stem_md: The line $3x + 4y - 12 = 0$ cuts the $y$-axis at a height of
questions.solution_md: On the $y$-axis $x = 0$, so $4y - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow y = 3$. Option (c) is where the line cuts the $x$-axis, (d) has the wrong sign and (a) is the constant term.

questions.stem_md: Which equation describes the line of slope $3$ passing through $(-1, 2)$?
questions.solution_md: Point-slope form: $y - 2 = 3(x + 1) \Rightarrow y - 2 = 3x + 3 \Rightarrow 3x - y + 5 = 0$. Option (d) is the line of slope $3$ through $(1, -2)$, (a) has slope $-3$ and (b) has slope $\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: The line joining $A(0, -3)$ and $B(4, 5)$ has the equation
questions.solution_md: Slope $m = \dfrac{5 - (-3)}{4 - 0} = 2$, and $A$ is on the $y$-axis, so $c = -3$: the line is $y = 2x - 3$. Option (a) has the wrong sign of the slope, (b) the wrong sign of the intercept and (c) the slope upside down.

questions.stem_md: Which of these lines is parallel to $2x - 3y + 4 = 0$?
questions.solution_md: The given line has slope $\dfrac{2}{3}$. The line $4x - 6y - 1 = 0$ has slope $\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ too, and a different intercept, so it is parallel. Option (c) has slope $-\dfrac{3}{2}$ and is perpendicular to the given line; (b) and (d) have slopes $\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $-\dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem_md: A line is drawn at right angles to the segment joining $(1, 4)$ and $(5, 2)$. What is its slope?
questions.solution_md: The segment has slope $\dfrac{2 - 4}{5 - 1} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. A perpendicular slope multiplies with it to give $-1$: $-\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 = -1$, so the answer is $2$. Option (a) is the slope of the segment itself, and (c) changes its sign without inverting it.

questions.stem_md: For what value of $k$ is the line $3x + ky - 2 = 0$ parallel to $6x - 4y + 1 = 0$?
questions.solution_md: Parallel lines have equal slopes: $-\dfrac{3}{k} = \dfrac{6}{4} \Rightarrow 6k = -12 \Rightarrow k = -2$. Option (a) is the value that makes the two lines perpendicular, and (d) loses the minus sign.

questions.stem_md: Find $p$ so that the lines $px - 2y + 5 = 0$ and $4x + 6y - 1 = 0$ cut each other at right angles.
questions.solution_md: The slopes are $\dfrac{p}{2}$ and $-\dfrac{4}{6} = -\dfrac{2}{3}$. For perpendicular lines their product is $-1$: $\dfrac{p}{2} \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -1 \Rightarrow p = 3$. Option (b) makes the slopes equal, which gives parallel lines instead.

questions.stem_md: Which equation is the perpendicular bisector of the segment from $(2, 5)$ to $(6, 1)$?
questions.solution_md: The mid-point is $(4, 3)$, since $\dfrac{2 + 6}{2} = 4$ and $\dfrac{5 + 1}{2} = 3$. The segment has slope $\dfrac{1 - 5}{6 - 2} = -1$, so the bisector has slope $1$: $y - 3 = x - 4$, that is $x - y - 1 = 0$. Option (b) is the line through the two given points.

questions.solution_md: On the $x$-axis $y = 0$, so $2x = 10$ and $x = 5$: the point is $(5, 0)$. Option (b) is where the line meets the $y$-axis.

questions.stem_md: Find the equation of the line joining $(-2, 7)$ and $(4, -5)$, and the point where it meets the $x$-axis.

Point-slope form with $(-2, 7)$: $y - 7 = -2(x + 2) \Rightarrow y - 7 = -2x - 4 \Rightarrow 2x + y - 3 = 0$.

On the $x$-axis $y = 0$: $2x = 3$, so the line meets it at $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right)$.

questions.stem_md: Find the equation of the line through $(5, 1)$ that is perpendicular to $2x + 5y - 3 = 0$.

The given line is $y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x + \dfrac{3}{5}$, with slope $-\dfrac{2}{5}$.

A perpendicular has slope $\dfrac{5}{2}$, because $-\dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{5}{2} = -1$.

Through $(5, 1)$: $y - 1 = \dfrac{5}{2}(x - 5) \Rightarrow 2y - 2 = 5x - 25 \Rightarrow 5x - 2y - 23 = 0$.

$\dfrac{9 - k}{3 - (-1)} = 2 \Rightarrow 9 - k = 8 \Rightarrow k = 1$.

Using $B$: $y - 9 = 2(x - 3) \Rightarrow y = 2x + 3$.

questions.stem_md: $P(-4, 1)$ and $Q(2, 5)$ are two points. Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $PQ$.

answer.model_answer_md:
Mid-point $M$: $\dfrac{-4 + 2}{2} = -1$ and $\dfrac{1 + 5}{2} = 3$, so $M(-1, 3)$.

Slope of $PQ$: $\dfrac{5 - 1}{2 - (-4)} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$; the bisector has slope $-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Through $M$: $y - 3 = -\dfrac{3}{2}(x + 1) \Rightarrow 2y - 6 = -3x - 3 \Rightarrow 3x + 2y - 3 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: The perpendicular bisector goes through the mid-point with the negative reciprocal slope.

questions.stem_md: Find the point where $3x - y = 5$ and $x + 2y = 4$ intersect, and the equation of the line through it parallel to $2x + 5y = 1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
From the first equation $y = 3x - 5$. Substituting: $x + 2(3x - 5) = 4 \Rightarrow 7x = 14 \Rightarrow x = 2$, and then $y = 3 \times 2 - 5 = 1$. They meet at $(2, 1)$.

The line $2x + 5y = 1$ has slope $-\dfrac{2}{5}$, so the parallel line has the same slope.

Through $(2, 1)$: $y - 1 = -\dfrac{2}{5}(x - 2) \Rightarrow 5y - 5 = -2x + 4 \Rightarrow 2x + 5y - 9 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Solve the pair by substitution; a parallel line keeps the slope.

The points are $A(-3, -2)$, $B(1, 6)$ and $C(4, 12)$.

(ii) Find the equation of the line through them.

(ii) $y - 6 = 2(x - 1) \Rightarrow 2x - y + 4 = 0$.

(iii) Putting $x = 0$: $y = 4$, so the line cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, 4)$.

questions.solution_md: Equal slopes through a common point mean the three points are on one line; then use the point-slope form.

The line $3x - 5y + 30 = 0$ meets the $x$-axis at $P$ and the $y$-axis at $Q$.

(i) Find $P$ and $Q$.

(ii) Find the slope of $PQ$.

(iii) Find the area of triangle $OPQ$, where $O$ is the origin.

(ii) $5y = 3x + 30 \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{3}{5}x + 6$, so the slope is $\dfrac{3}{5}$.

(iii) $OP = 10$ and $OQ = 6$ lie along the axes, at right angles: area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 6 = 30$ square units.

questions.stem_md:
The lines $ax + 3y - 6 = 0$ and $2x - y + 3 = 0$ are given.

(i) Find $a$ if the lines are parallel.

(ii) Find $a$ if the lines are perpendicular.

(iii) For the value in (i), find the $y$-intercept of each line and explain why the lines do not coincide.

answer.model_answer_md:
The first line has slope $-\dfrac{a}{3}$ and the second, $y = 2x + 3$, has slope $2$.

(i) $-\dfrac{a}{3} = 2 \Rightarrow a = -6$.

(ii) $-\dfrac{a}{3} \times 2 = -1 \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

(iii) With $a = -6$ the first line is $-6x + 3y - 6 = 0$, that is $y = 2x + 2$, with $y$-intercept $2$; the second has $y$-intercept $3$. Equal slopes but different intercepts: the lines are parallel and never meet.

questions.solution_md: Equal slopes for parallel lines, product $-1$ for perpendicular ones; parallel lines with different intercepts are distinct.

questions.stem_md:
Triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(1, 4)$, $B(-3, -2)$ and $C(5, 0)$.

(i) Find the equation of the median through $B$.

(ii) Find the centroid $G$ of the triangle and show that it lies on this median.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Mid-point of $AC$: $\dfrac{1 + 5}{2} = 3$ and $\dfrac{4 + 0}{2} = 2$, so $D(3, 2)$. Slope of $BD$: $\dfrac{2 - (-2)}{3 - (-3)} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. Median: $y + 2 = \dfrac{2}{3}(x + 3) \Rightarrow 3y + 6 = 2x + 6 \Rightarrow 2x - 3y = 0$.

(ii) $G$ has coordinates $\dfrac{1 + (-3) + 5}{3} = 1$ and $\dfrac{4 + (-2) + 0}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $G\left(1, \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$.

Substituting $G$ in $2x - 3y = 0$: $2 \times 1 - 3 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 0$, so $G$ lies on the median, as every median passes through the centroid.

questions.solution_md: The median from $B$ joins $B$ to the mid-point of $AC$; the centroid is the average of the three vertices.

questions.stem_md:
In triangle $PQR$, $P(0, 4)$, $Q(-4, -3)$ and $R(6, 2)$.

(i) Find the slope of $QR$.

(ii) Find the equation of the altitude from $P$.

(iii) Find the foot of this altitude on $QR$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) $m_{QR} = \dfrac{2 - (-3)}{6 - (-4)} = \dfrac{5}{10} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

(ii) The altitude is perpendicular to $QR$, so its slope is $-2$: $y - 4 = -2(x - 0) \Rightarrow 2x + y - 4 = 0$.

(iii) Line $QR$: $y - 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x - 6) \Rightarrow x - 2y - 2 = 0$. From the altitude, $y = 4 - 2x$; substituting: $x - 2(4 - 2x) - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow 5x = 10 \Rightarrow x = 2$, and then $y = 0$.

The foot of the altitude is $(2, 0)$.

questions.solution_md: An altitude passes through a vertex at right angles to the opposite side; its foot is where it meets that side.

questions.stem_md: $A(2, -1)$, $B(6, 1)$, $C(4, 5)$ and $D(0, 3)$ are the vertices of a quadrilateral. Using slopes only, show that $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

answer.model_answer_md:
$m_{AB} = \dfrac{1 - (-1)}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $m_{DC} = \dfrac{5 - 3}{4 - 0} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $AB \parallel DC$.

$m_{BC} = \dfrac{5 - 1}{4 - 6} = -2$ and $m_{AD} = \dfrac{3 - (-1)}{0 - 2} = -2$, so $BC \parallel AD$. Hence $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

$m_{AB} \times m_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (-2) = -1$, so $AB \perp BC$.

A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle.

questions.solution_md: Two pairs of parallel sides make a parallelogram; one pair of perpendicular adjacent sides makes it a rectangle.

questions.stem_md:
$A(-1, -4)$ and $B(3, 0)$ are two points. Show all working.

(a) Find the slope and the inclination of $AB$.

(b) Find the equation of $AB$ and the intercepts it makes on the two axes.

(c) The point $C(k, 5)$ lies on $AB$. Find $k$, and the equation of the line through $C$ whose $y$-intercept is $-1$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $m = \dfrac{0 - (-4)}{3 - (-1)} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1$. Since $\tan \theta = 1$, the inclination is $\theta = 45^\circ$.

**(b)** Through $B$: $y - 0 = 1(x - 3) \Rightarrow x - y - 3 = 0$. Putting $y = 0$ gives $x = 3$; putting $x = 0$ gives $y = -3$. So the $x$-intercept is $3$ and the $y$-intercept is $-3$.

**(c)** $C$ satisfies $x - y - 3 = 0$: $k - 5 - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow k = 8$, so $C(8, 5)$. The required line passes through $C(8, 5)$ and $(0, -1)$, so its slope is $\dfrac{5 - (-1)}{8 - 0} = \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$, and $y = \dfrac{3}{4}x - 1 \Rightarrow 3x - 4y - 4 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Two-point slope, then the inclination from tan θ = m; intercepts from x = 0 and y = 0; a point on a line satisfies its equation; a y-intercept of −1 is the point (0, −1).

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) Find the equation of the line $L_1$ through $(2, 5)$ and $(-1, -1)$.

(b) $Q$ is the point $(5, 1)$. Find the equations of the line $L_2$ through $Q$ parallel to $L_1$, and of the line $L_3$ through $Q$ perpendicular to $L_1$.

(c) $L_1$ and $L_3$ meet at $F$. Find $F$, and the point $Q'$ for which $F$ is the mid-point of $QQ'$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Slope: $m = \dfrac{-1 - 5}{-1 - 2} = \dfrac{-6}{-3} = 2$. Then $y - 5 = 2(x - 2) \Rightarrow 2x - y + 1 = 0$.

**(b)** $L_2$ has slope $2$: $y - 1 = 2(x - 5) \Rightarrow 2x - y - 9 = 0$. $L_3$ has slope $-\dfrac{1}{2}$: $y - 1 = -\dfrac{1}{2}(x - 5) \Rightarrow 2y - 2 = -x + 5 \Rightarrow x + 2y - 7 = 0$.

**(c)** From $L_1$, $y = 2x + 1$; substituting in $L_3$: $x + 2(2x + 1) - 7 = 0 \Rightarrow 5x = 5 \Rightarrow x = 1$, and $y = 3$. So $F(1, 3)$.

If $F$ is the mid-point of $QQ'$, then $Q'$ has coordinates $2 \times 1 - 5 = -3$ and $2 \times 3 - 1 = 5$: $Q'(-3, 5)$.

questions.solution_md: Parallel lines keep the slope and perpendicular lines take the negative reciprocal; solve L1 with L3 by substitution; reverse the mid-point formula: x2 = 2x − x1.

questions.stem_md:
The vertices of triangle $ABC$ are $A(-4, -1)$, $B(5, 6)$ and $C(1, -6)$. Show all working.

(a) Find the equation of the side $BC$.

(b) Find the equation of the median through $A$.

(c) Find the equation of the altitude through $A$, and the coordinates of its foot on $BC$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $m_{BC} = \dfrac{-6 - 6}{1 - 5} = \dfrac{-12}{-4} = 3$. Through $B$: $y - 6 = 3(x - 5) \Rightarrow 3x - y - 9 = 0$.

**(b)** Mid-point $D$ of $BC$: $\dfrac{5 + 1}{2} = 3$ and $\dfrac{6 + (-6)}{2} = 0$, so $D(3, 0)$. Slope of $AD$: $\dfrac{0 - (-1)}{3 - (-4)} = \dfrac{1}{7}$. Median: $y + 1 = \dfrac{1}{7}(x + 4) \Rightarrow 7y + 7 = x + 4 \Rightarrow x - 7y - 3 = 0$.

**(c)** The altitude is perpendicular to $BC$, so its slope is $-\dfrac{1}{3}$: $y + 1 = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4) \Rightarrow 3y + 3 = -x - 4 \Rightarrow x + 3y + 7 = 0$.

Foot: from $BC$, $y = 3x - 9$; substituting in the altitude: $x + 3(3x - 9) + 7 = 0 \Rightarrow 10x = 20 \Rightarrow x = 2$, and $y = 3 \times 2 - 9 = -3$. The foot is $(2, -3)$.

questions.solution_md: A median joins a vertex to the mid-point of the opposite side; an altitude passes through a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side, and its foot is found by solving the two equations together.

questions.stem_md:
$A(-3, 7)$ and $B(6, -5)$ are given. Show all working.

(a) The point $P$ divides $AB$ internally in the ratio $1 : 2$. Find $P$.

(b) Find the slope of $AB$, and the equation of the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$.

(c) The line found in (b) meets the $x$-axis at $Q$. Find $Q$, and the equation of the line through $Q$ parallel to $AB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** By the section formula with $m : n = 1 : 2$: $x = \dfrac{1 \times 6 + 2 \times (-3)}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{0}{3} = 0$ and $y = \dfrac{1 \times (-5) + 2 \times 7}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3$. So $P(0, 3)$, a point on the $y$-axis.

**(b)** $m_{AB} = \dfrac{-5 - 7}{6 - (-3)} = \dfrac{-12}{9} = -\dfrac{4}{3}$. The perpendicular has slope $\dfrac{3}{4}$, and passes through $P(0, 3)$: $y - 3 = \dfrac{3}{4}x \Rightarrow 3x - 4y + 12 = 0$.

**(c)** Putting $y = 0$: $3x + 12 = 0$, so $x = -4$ and $Q(-4, 0)$. The parallel line has slope $-\dfrac{4}{3}$: $y - 0 = -\dfrac{4}{3}(x + 4) \Rightarrow 4x + 3y + 16 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Section formula for P; negative reciprocal slope for the perpendicular; y = 0 for the x-axis; a parallel line keeps the slope of AB.

questions.stem_md:
$A(-1, 2)$, $B(3, 4)$ and $C(5, 0)$ are three vertices of a parallelogram $ABCD$. Show all working.

(a) Use the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other to find $D$.

(b) Using slopes, show that $ABCD$ is in fact a rectangle.

(c) Find the equation of the diagonal $BD$, and of the line through $A$ parallel to $BD$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The mid-point of $AC$ has coordinates $\dfrac{-1 + 5}{2} = 2$ and $\dfrac{2 + 0}{2} = 1$, that is $(2, 1)$. It is also the mid-point of $BD$, so $D$ has coordinates $2 \times 2 - 3 = 1$ and $2 \times 1 - 4 = -2$: $D(1, -2)$.

**(b)** $m_{AB} = \dfrac{4 - 2}{3 - (-1)} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $m_{BC} = \dfrac{0 - 4}{5 - 3} = -2$, so $m_{AB} \times m_{BC} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times (-2) = -1$ and $AB \perp BC$. A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle.

**(c)** $m_{BD} = \dfrac{-2 - 4}{1 - 3} = 3$, so $BD$ is $y - 4 = 3(x - 3) \Rightarrow 3x - y - 5 = 0$. The line through $A$ with the same slope is $y - 2 = 3(x + 1) \Rightarrow 3x - y + 5 = 0$.

questions.solution_md: Reverse the mid-point formula for D; a right angle at B turns the parallelogram into a rectangle; a parallel line keeps the slope.

questions.stem_md:
The line $3x - 2y + 12 = 0$ meets the $x$-axis at $A$ and the $y$-axis at $B$. Show all working.

(a) Find $A$, $B$ and the slope of $AB$.

(b) Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.

(c) The perpendicular bisector meets the $x$-axis at $C$. Find $C$ and verify that $CA = CB$.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $y = 0$: $3x = -12$, so $A(-4, 0)$. $x = 0$: $2y = 12$, so $B(0, 6)$. Slope of $AB$: $\dfrac{6 - 0}{0 - (-4)} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

**(b)** Mid-point of $AB$: $\dfrac{-4 + 0}{2} = -2$ and $\dfrac{0 + 6}{2} = 3$, so $M(-2, 3)$. The bisector has slope $-\dfrac{2}{3}$: $y - 3 = -\dfrac{2}{3}(x + 2) \Rightarrow 3y - 9 = -2x - 4 \Rightarrow 2x + 3y - 5 = 0$.

**(c)** $y = 0$: $2x = 5$, so $C\left(\dfrac{5}{2}, 0\right)$.

$CA$ lies along the $x$-axis: $CA = \dfrac{5}{2} - (-4) = \dfrac{13}{2}$. $CB = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{169}{4}} = \dfrac{13}{2}$. So $CA = CB$, as it must be for every point of the perpendicular bisector.

questions.solution_md: Intercepts from x = 0 and y = 0; the perpendicular bisector passes through the mid-point with the negative reciprocal slope; any point on it is equidistant from A and B (distance formula).

questions.stem_md:
Two lines are $L_1: 2x - y - 1 = 0$ and $L_2: x + y - 5 = 0$. Show all working.

(a) Write the slope and $y$-intercept of each line, and find the point $P$ where they meet.

(b) Find the equation of the line $OP$, where $O$ is the origin, and show that it is perpendicular to $2x + 3y - 6 = 0$.

(c) $L_2$ meets the $x$-axis at $R$. Find $R$, and the equation of the line through $R$ parallel to $L_1$; state where this line cuts the $y$-axis.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $L_1$: $y = 2x - 1$, slope $2$, $y$-intercept $-1$. $L_2$: $y = -x + 5$, slope $-1$, $y$-intercept $5$. Adding the two equations: $3x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow x = 2$, and then $y = 5 - 2 = 3$. So $P(2, 3)$.

**(b)** $OP$ has slope $\dfrac{3}{2}$: $y = \dfrac{3}{2}x \Rightarrow 3x - 2y = 0$. The line $2x + 3y - 6 = 0$ has slope $-\dfrac{2}{3}$, and $\dfrac{3}{2} \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = -1$, so the lines are perpendicular.

**(c)** $y = 0$ in $L_2$ gives $x = 5$, so $R(5, 0)$. Through $R$ with slope $2$: $y - 0 = 2(x - 5) \Rightarrow 2x - y - 10 = 0$. Putting $x = 0$: $y = -10$, so it cuts the $y$-axis at $(0, -10)$.

questions.solution_md: Read slopes and intercepts from y = mx + c; add the equations to eliminate y; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1; a parallel line keeps the slope.
